claims.text: The melt-spun Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 alloy exhibits multiple primary non-eutectic crystalline phases.
The alloy exhibits a multistep crystallization sequence.
The alloy undergoes extensive primary crystallization during slower cooling and conventional reheating.
Crystallization occurs even after rapid cooling when the alloy is subsequently heated conventionally at a slower rate.
Applying pulsed laser flash annealing immediately after melt spinning will suppress nucleation of primary crystalline phases.
Pulsed laser flash annealing will increase the homogeneity of the undercooled or supercooled material.
Pulsed laser flash annealing will increase amorphous retention.
Pulsed laser flash annealing will increase the thermal stability of the amorphous structure.
A microsecond-to-millisecond pulse reaching just above Tg can produce structural relaxation while avoiding prolonged diffusion and nucleation.
The treatment will reduce the density of heterogeneous nucleation sites in the amorphous matrix.
The treatment will create a more relaxed atomic configuration that retards diffusion associated with primary-phase nucleation.
Momentary heating above Tg will reset structural inhomogeneities induced during solidification.
Resetting structural inhomogeneities will enhance glass-forming ability during subsequent thermal exposure.
Relative to conventionally reheated samples, laser-treated samples will have a higher crystallization-onset temperature Tx.
The intervention requires prior melt spinning at a cooling rate greater than approximately 10^5 K/s.
Excessive laser-pulse duration or energy may promote crystallization rather than suppress it.
A high-purity argon atmosphere will avoid oxidation during laser treatment.
